common_name: Tropicanna Black Canna (Near-Black Foliage Tropical Canna)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant once soil has warmed above 60°F; Tropicanna Black is grown chiefly for its near-black, deep maroon-purple foliage rather than for flower impact.

directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, where the strongest light produces the darkest, glossiest foliage color. Tropicanna Black carries broad, paddle-shaped leaves in a deep purple-black tone that reads almost black from a distance, offering a striking contrast partner for the brighter-leaved Tropicanna and Tropicanna Gold in the same series, with orange-red flowers appearing above the foliage through summer. Feed monthly and keep soil evenly moist, since cannas are heavy feeders that sulk in dry, lean conditions. In zone 9 and warmer it overwinters in place; in colder zones lift and store rhizomes after frost blackens the foliage.
sources: American Canna Society
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Canna Growing Guide

common_name: Tropical Salmon Canna (Compact Seed-Grown Salmon-Pink Canna)

planting.note: Set out transplants or divided rhizomes after the last frost in rich, moist soil in full sun; part of the compact Tropical series, which blooms earlier in its first year than traditional tall heirloom cannas.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun and feed regularly to sustain its long bloom season. Tropical Salmon bears warm salmon-pink flowers over plain green foliage on a short, bushy plant, sharing the compact first-year-flowering habit of its Tropical series relatives Tropical Rose and Tropical Bronze Scarlet but in a softer, sunset-toned color. Its shorter stature suits bedding schemes and large containers where taller heirloom cannas would crowd out neighboring plants. Deadhead spent stalks to encourage continued flowering through the season.

common_name: Tropical Yellow Canna (Compact Seed-Grown Yellow Canna)

planting.note: Set out transplants or divided rhizomes after the last frost in rich, moist soil in full sun; a Tropical-series canna bred for a compact, bushy habit and reliable first-year bloom.

directions: Grow in rich, evenly moist soil in full sun, feeding monthly to keep the compact plants blooming steadily. Tropical Yellow produces clear, bright yellow flowers over plain green foliage on a shorter, denser plant than tall heirloom cannas, making it a practical choice for mass bedding or mixed container plantings where a smaller footprint is needed. It shares the Tropical series' trait of flowering in its first season from seed-propagated stock, unlike slower-establishing rhizome-only heirloom types. Keep soil consistently moist but well drained to prevent rhizome rot.

common_name: Pink President Canna (Heirloom Soft Pink Large-Flowered Canna)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring and plant once soil has warmed; Pink President is a pink-flowered counterpart to the classic red 'President' canna, sharing its sturdy, compact habit.

directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun, feeding monthly during the growing season for the fullest flower display. Pink President carries large, rounded, soft pink blooms over broad green foliage on a sturdier, more compact plant than many taller heirloom cannas, making it easier to work into a mixed perennial border without staking. Like its red sibling 'President', it is a long-cultivated garden standby valued for dependable, heavy flowering over a long season. In zone 9 and warmer it overwinters in the ground; elsewhere lift and store rhizomes after frost.

common_name: Indian Shot Canna (Pendant Pink-Flowered Species Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes once soil has warmed in rich, moist soil in full sun to part shade; this wild Andean species carries large, pendant flower clusters distinct from the upright blooms of most garden hybrid cannas.

directions: Grow in consistently moist, rich soil in full sun to light shade, siting plants where their tall, arching stems have room to display their drooping flower clusters. Canna iridiflora, native to the Andes of Peru and Ecuador, is a large species canna notable for its nodding, rose-pink flowers held in pendant clusters at the stem tips, a distinctly different presentation from the upright, outward-facing blooms of most modern hybrid cannas. Its height and dramatic flower form make it best suited to the back of a border or as a specimen where its unusual habit can be appreciated up close. This species has long been used by breeders as a source of flower-form diversity in canna hybridizing programs.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes once soil has warmed in rich, moist soil in full sun; this Central American species canna has dark purple-red foliage and small red flowers, and is cited in canna breeding literature as a source of dark-foliage genetics.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, where the richest foliage color develops. Canna warszewiczii is a smaller wild species from Central America grown mainly for its dusky, dark purple-red foliage rather than its modest small red flowers, offering a more restrained scale than the large tropical-foliage hybrids derived in part from it. It spreads by rhizome into a tidy clump and suits a mixed border or container where a dark-leaved accent is wanted without the bulk of a full-size hybrid canna. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing season and reduce watering once foliage dies back for winter storage in colder zones.

common_name: Cannova Bronze Scarlet Canna (Dark-Foliage Seed-Grown Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes or seed-grown transplants once soil has warmed; Cannova Bronze Scarlet pairs bronze-purple foliage with scarlet blooms in the compact, weather-tolerant Cannova series.

directions: Plant rhizomes or transplants in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun, feeding monthly for strong foliage color and continuous bloom. Cannova Bronze Scarlet combines bronze-purple foliage with bright scarlet flowers on the same sturdy, wind-resistant stems that distinguish the Cannova series from older, taller canna cultivars, giving it a darker, more dramatic look than the plain-green-leaved colors in the same line. Its compact size suits containers and front-of-border placement where taller bronze-leaved heirloom cannas would be out of scale. It overwinters in the ground in zone 9 and warmer; elsewhere lift and store rhizomes after frost.

common_name: Cannova Red Canna (Compact Weather-Tolerant Red Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes or seed-grown transplants once soil has warmed; Cannova Red bears true red blooms over clean green foliage in the compact, storm-resistant Cannova series.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun, feeding monthly through the growing season for steady bloom. Cannova Red produces clear, vivid red flowers over plain green foliage on the same compact, sturdy-stemmed plant as other Cannova colors, holding up well to wind and heavy summer rain that can flatten taller, older canna cultivars. Its shorter stature makes it a practical choice for mass plantings, mixed borders, and large containers alike. It overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer; in colder zones lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store dry over winter.

common_name: Cannova Orange Canna (Compact Weather-Tolerant Orange Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes or seed-grown transplants once soil has warmed; Cannova Orange bears bright orange blooms over clean green foliage in the compact, storm-resistant Cannova series.

directions: Grow in rich, evenly moist soil in full sun, feeding monthly to sustain bloom production through summer. Cannova Orange bears bright, warm orange flowers over plain green foliage on the same compact, wind-tolerant plant as other Cannova colors, making it easy to combine with the series' scarlet, red, and bronze-scarlet selections for a multicolor summer bed. Its tidy habit and sturdy stems reduce the need for staking compared with taller heirloom canna cultivars. Provide excellent drainage along with consistent moisture, since standing water leads to rhizome rot.

common_name: Toucan Coral Canna (Compact Heat and Humidity-Tolerant Coral Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes or vegetatively-propagated transplants once soil has warmed; Toucan Coral is part of a compact Proven Winners canna series bred for uniform habit and strong heat and humidity tolerance.

directions: Plant rhizomes or transplants a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun. Toucan Coral produces soft coral-orange blooms above lush, tropical-textured green foliage, offering a gentler color than the vivid scarlet of its series mate Toucan Scarlet while keeping the same compact, uniform habit bred for containers and smaller garden beds. It is a heavy feeder and needs consistent moisture paired with excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot. It overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer; elsewhere, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.

common_name: Flevo Smiley Gladiolus (Compact Bicolor Spray Gladiolus)

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed; Flevo Smiley is a compact, multi-branching Dutch-bred spray gladiolus with bicolor blooms marked by a distinct contrasting blotch.

directions: Plant corms in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them closely for a fuller display of the branching flower spikes. Flevo Smiley produces smaller, more numerous blooms per stem than large-flowered exhibition gladiolus, each marked with a contrasting throat blotch that gives the open flower a face-like pattern, part of a group of modern Dutch garden and cut-flower gladiolus bred for a shorter, bushier habit than traditional tall hybrids. The compact branching habit suits mixed borders and cutting gardens alike, producing multiple stems per corm without staking in most garden settings. Lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall in regions colder than zone 8.
sources: North American Gladiolus Council
Dutch flower bulb trade reference

common_name: Hunting Song Gladiolus (Heirloom Deep Red Large-Flowered Gladiolus)

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, staggering plantings for a longer bloom season; Hunting Song is a deep red heirloom gladiolus preserved and sold by heirloom bulb specialists.

directions: Plant corms in well-drained soil in full sun and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes. Hunting Song bears deep, velvety red blooms on sturdy stems, an older American gladiolus variety that has persisted in cultivation through heirloom bulb exchanges even as it fell out of the commercial trade in favor of newer introductions. Cut spikes once the lowest florets show color for indoor arrangements, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.
sources: Old House Gardens heirloom bulb reference
